figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. Left: ETH/UCY LOO: revealing k=8 observations contracts HProbZ’s predictive std by 23.6% through joint posterior updates over shared (β, α), vs. 3.6% for a samecapacity Gaussian mixture (weight reweighting only); mean over 3 seeds. Right: schematic at k=0 vs k=6: each HProbZ hexagon is c+Gbβ+Gdα inflated by the 2σ halo of Gsν. Downstream (nuScenes, N=39,829, 6 s, static obstacle): at near-matched 10% FAR HProbZ produces 30% fewer trajectory-level collisions than same-encoder MDN-K2 (Tab. 5); per-step reverses.

Figure 2: Empirical fingerprint of Theorem 2 (1-D HProbZ with a=2, σ=0.3, 105 samples). Left: GMMs (K=1, . . . ,64) visually approximate the density. Middle: at the sinc-zero frequencies tk = kπ/a, |ϕGMM| plateaus at ∼ 2−5×10−3 regardless of K — the structural signature the proof predicts no finite GMM can erase. Right: matching HProbZ’s held-out NLL with a finite GMM requires K=8 (23 free density parameters) vs HProbZ’s 2, an 11.5× ratio. Full setup in App. C.

Figure 3: Structural-property validation on trained HProbZ models. Left: nuScenes speed-stratified generator norms (log-y) — ∥Gb∥ scales ∼ 370× stationary→high-speed, ∥Gs∥ scales ∼ 94×, ∥Gd∥ stays within 5.4×, so the three generators track interpretable, qualitatively distinct uncertainty sources (Theorem 3; setup App. D.17). Middle: entropy-gap CDF across 13,000+ samples on three benchmarks; all curves lie strictly below the theoretical bound 1 2 log(πe/6)≈0.1765 nats/dim (red dashed). Right: per-dataset distribution of the same gap (symmetric log scale). Zero violations on any benchmark for Proposition 5 (App. C.4).

Table 3: nuScenes minADE (m): published map-aware baselines, trajectory-only d=128 controlled sweep (3 seeds), and d=256 matched-encoder. MDN-K2†: best-tuned (App. D.22). Seed asymmetry in the d=256 block : HProbZ is mean±std over 14 seeds (App. D.24); MDN-K2 row is single-seed (no ±std), so the 46% gap is HProbZ’s 14-seed mean vs one MDN-K2 seed.

Table 7: Conformal set volume comparison (α=0.1, D=24, within-scene calibration). All methods reach ∼ 90% coverage; HProbZ-CP is 5.5/3.9 orders smaller than StdCP/MDN-CP on the ETH/UCY average and 16.3/13.9 orders smaller on Argoverse 2. HOTEL is a counter-example: MDN-CP is 3.5 OOM smaller than HProbZ-CP there (App. D.4 discusses the mechanism). Bold marks the smallest volume per row.

Figure 4: Relative gap (Vrelaxed − Vtrue)/Vtrue between the Gaussian-relaxed posterior variance (closed-form) and the true uniform-prior posterior variance (grid integration, 1,000 MC reps), as a function of revealed observations k and Fisher-information ratio κ. All 16 cells lie inside the ±10% band; the relaxation slightly over-estimates the true variance, so contraction reported in the body is conservative relative to the true uniform-prior posterior.

Figure 5: Controlled generator sweeps under exact vs. Gaussian-approximate likelihood; mean±std over 5 seeds. Left: mode sweep (K=1→7): both likelihoods identify modal structure via Gb. Middle: drift sweep: the exact likelihood routes drift to Gd (∆∥Gd∥=2.90 ≫ ∆∥Gs∥=2.27, ∆∥Gb∥=0.73); the Gaussian approximation reverses the dominance (∆∥Gs∥=2.70 wins), confirming Prop. 4. Right: noise sweep: ∥Gs∥ tracks σ monotonically; residual Gd/Gs degeneracy is halved by the kurtosis regulariser (App. D.7). Per-value tables below.

Table 11: Drift sweep: exact vs. Gaussian approximation (fixed 3 modes, noise 0.15, 5 random seeds ∈ {42, 123, 456, 789, 2026}, mean ± std, sym-broken Gb initialisation per Appendix D.24). Under the exact likelihood, ∥Gb∥ remains essentially flat (∆=0.73) while ∆∥Gd∥=2.90 dominates—drift is correctly routed to the bounded generator. Under the Gaussian approximation, ∆∥Gs∥=2.70 dominates instead, confirming Proposition 4: the surrogate misattributes bounded variance to the stochastic component.
Figure 6: All 10 seeds recover ground-truth HProbZ parameters; per-seed error below 0.004.

Table 12: Noise sweep: exact vs. Gaussian approximation (fixed 3 modes, drift 0.3, 200 epochs, mean±std over 5 seeds ∈ {42, 123, 456, 789, 2026}). ∥Gs∥ rises monotonically with σ under both likelihoods. Residual Gd/Gs degeneracy is addressed separately by the kurtosis regulariser (App. D.7, Tab. 19).

Table 14: Per-seed CRPS on nuScenes for matched (HProbZ, MDN-K2) pairs. HProbZ stays in [0.80, 0.86] across all five seeds; MDN-K2 spans [0.66, 0.92]. Means are statistically tied (95% paired-bootstrap CI on the gap [−0.07,+0.07], contains 0); HProbZ is tighter on every spread metric we computed on these 5 seeds (sample-std 4.5×, IQR 2.6×, MAD 9.6×, range 5.0×), but with n=5 the std-ratio bootstrap CI is wide ([0.9×, 45×], contains unity), so this is a directional observation rather than an established gap. Robustness diagnostics in the paragraph below. All numbers reproducible via the CRPS evaluation script in the supplementary code.

Figure 7: HProbZ achieves the highest coverage when the data-generating uncertainty is non-trivial (Medium and High regimes, ≥ 0.997) while maintaining competitive FDE. In the Low regime, HProbZ’s tight intervals trade coverage for compactness; variance-based baselines reach the 95% target there only by inflating volume far beyond what the small intrinsic noise warrants.

Figure 8: HProbZ’s modal acquisition signal improves test NLL; MDN total-variance acquisition and random selection both degrade. Scope: comparison is HProbZ-∥Gb∥ vs MDN-total-variance vs random under a single acquisition recipe; standard Bayesian-acquisition baselines (BALD, BatchBALD, ensemble disagreement) are not included, and the negative MDN result is specific to the total-variance signal. We report this as a structural-decomposition demonstration, not a horse-race against the AL literature.

Table 16: OOD conformal coverage: HProbZ maintains calibration under distribution shift. ETH/UCY uses leave-one-out (train on 4, test on 1). nuScenes calibrates on low-speed, evaluates on both low-speed (IID) and high-speed (OOD).

Table 17: Encoder scaling on ETH/UCY (mean±std over 5 seeds). Across all three encoder sizes (110K–2.4M parameters), HProbZ’s minADE is ∼ 21% lower than MDN-K20’s; the ADE gap is stable across capacity. On minFDE the comparison reverses: MDN-K20 wins by 0.06–0.09m at every capacity (bolded entries). Net read: in this vanilla protocol HProbZ is sample-efficient on full-trajectory accuracy and MDN-K20 is sharper on endpoint; the social-attention encoder used for the SOTA-chase row of Tab. 26 closes the FDE gap.

Table 20: Effect of binary generator count nb on ETH/UCY (aggregate over 5 scenes, best-mode ADE/FDE in meters, mean±std over 3 seeds). Increasing nb monotonically improves displacement metrics while adding negligible parameters.

Table 25: Controlled cross-method comparison on vanilla ETH/UCY (no Social attention; mean across 5 leave-one-out scenes). HProbZ achieves the best FDE@20 and inference latency among the four same-encoder configurations tested. Diffusion’s lower ADE at 50 DDIM steps is bought at ∼ 530× HProbZ’s inference cost; at matched single-pass inference budget (5 DDIM steps), Diffusion ADE rises by an order of magnitude. The diffusion baseline is not separately swept over noise schedule, denoiser depth, prediction target, or CFG (App. D.11).
Figure 9: HProbZ unifies existing prediction set types as special cases of a single parameterization.
Figure 10: ETH/UCY trajectory predictions with structurally interpretable binary-generator mode centers.

Figure 11: Qualitative visualization of HProbZ’s 2nb=8 binary-mode trajectories on three UNIV leave-one-out scenarios (nb=3, nd=1, nq=1). Solid colored lines are mode centers; faint lines are per-mode samples revealing the stochastic envelope; black dashed is ground truth. The structured decomposition produces well-separated modal branches that a Gaussian-mixture baseline would have to cover with a single inflated covariance.

Figure 12: HProbZ mode visualization on three HOTEL leave-one-out scenarios. The same binary generators produce qualitatively different mode branchings across scenes without supervision, demonstrating input-dependent structural discovery.

Figure 13: Planning cost vs. mode separation ∆y. The structured HProbZ planner transitions sharply at ∆y ≈ 4 and matches the oracle for ∆y ≥ 5, while scalar and MDN planners remain at the conservative SWERVE cost across all separations.

Table 28: ETH/UCY vs published methods (Avg minADE / minFDE @20, best-of-20, meters). Social HProbZ is competitive with recent SOTA on minADE; trails LED/Y-Net by ∼ 0.06m on minFDE. Among the listed methods, only HProbZ provides structured decomposition, conformal coverage, and refinement (this is a property of the listed set, not a literature-wide claim).
Table 29: Risk-estimate consistency on nuScenes (5,000 scenarios, 20 seeds). Full sample-budget sweep.

Table 31: MDN hyperparameter sweep on nuScenes (best-seed-of-3 per config, minADE in meters). Even the best-tuned MDN with full covariance does not match HProbZ. ∗HProbZ uses a discreteuniform-Gaussian convolution likelihood; its NLL is not on the same scale as the MDN mixture-density NLLs and is therefore omitted from this table (see Appendix C.6). †The K=8 entry shows the non-collapsed seed; under mode collapse the 3-seed mean is 3.134±0.225 ADE@10—see the dedicated K=8 sweep in Appendix D.27.

Table 33: Effect of sym-broken init strength on nuScenes minADE@10 (d=256, 4-layer encoder). Both sym-break sweeps use identical architecture and optimiser; only the Gb bias init differs. The b0=1.0 row is what the body reports.

Table 37: MDN-K=8 on nuScenes across three learning rates (3 seeds each), versus the existing MDN-K2 and HProbZ entries from Table 3. Even the best-tuned LR regresses by ∼ 1m below MDN-K2, consistent with classical mode-collapse: more components compete for limited data and produce dead modes.
